newsitem.title: USA: Europe must remove barriers to job growth-ministers.
newsitem.headline: Europe must remove barriers to job growth-ministers.

text.p: Europe's two leading economies need to tackle structural economic obstacles to job creation if they are to have any real hope of slashing painfully high unemployment, ministers said on Monday.

Speaking at the spring meeting of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, German and French finance ministers said their nations must press ahead with broad social-welfare reforms and that labour markets should be more flexible.
"The expected economic growth in 1997 will not be sufficient to noticeably reduce unemployment," German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said. "Unemployment in Germany is largely structural."
French Finance Minister Jean Arthuis echoed his German counterpart, saying Paris would continue to curb public spending.

"France is determined to continue this policy and deepen the structural reforms already undertaken to create new margins of growth for its economy in the medium term and thereby improve the labour situation," he said.

Europe has seen its unemployment rate steadily rachet higher in recent years with Germany and France posting unemployment rates of 11.3 percent and 12.8 percent respectively -- record highs that are more than double the U.S. rate.
Maybe most worrying for many European capitals, however, is that even amid signs of faster economic growth, there is little sign of a reduction in joblessness.

At issue is a generous social safety net enjoyed by many Europeans that dampens the pain of being unemployed and labour market practices that make it difficult for employers to adjust workforces to economic conditions.

Officials said they hoped to tackle structural obstacles to unemployment by reducing government spending. That could enable lower taxes, give economic growth a boost and make companies more willing to take on staff.
Speaking at different venues, Waigel and Arthuis said that unions and employers also needed to become more flexible in determining wages, benefits and employment levels.
Waigel, for example, called on German wage negotiators to drop ideological baggage and adopt contract agreements which would more closely reflect economic conditions.

Although many private economists agree with the unemployment prescriptions advocated by ministers here, calls for structural adjustments appeared also to reflect the self-interest of Waigel and Arthuis.
Leaner government is a hot issue in elections coming up in France and in Germany next autumn and both men have come under fire for not doing enough to bring unemployment down.
